task: Finalize this architecture decision record for the engineers and venue coordinators responsible for the Seatforge pilot.
source_facts: Seatforge is a fictional theater reservation service. This accepted pilot decision uses server-authoritative expiring seat holds. At most one active hold may exist for a seat within a particular performance. A standard hold lasts 120 seconds. The server clock determines expiration; browser clocks and countdown displays have no authority. A checkout succeeds against a hold only when payment authorization was recorded before that hold expired; a completion message arriving later may still succeed if the authorization was already recorded in time. A lost write quorum prevents creation of new holds, while the seat catalog remains readable. Availability in that catalog is observational and does not constitute ownership. A hold token maps to the original hold for 24 hours after creation. Repeating a request with the same token returns the original result and never extends its original deadline. Reusing a token for a different seat produces HOLD_KEY_CONFLICT. An expired hold is not revived by token replay. Venue coordinators alone may create accessibility holds, which last 240 seconds and cannot be renewed. Accessibility holds otherwise follow the same exclusivity, clock, and replay rules. Bulk seat blocks are outside the pilot. Hold tokens exclude buyer email; tracing uses the token rather than an email address. The pilot covers five venues. The performance gate is p95 hold-creation latency no greater than 180 ms at a sustained load of 600 requests per second. Expansion additionally requires seven consecutive days with zero double assignments. Double assignment means granting overlapping active holds for the same seat and performance. The team rejected browser-owned deadlines because differing client clocks cannot establish a shared expiry boundary. It rejected renewable standard holds because repeated extension could keep seats unavailable indefinitely. It rejected selling from cached catalog availability during a quorum outage because an observational read cannot enforce exclusivity. A global queue is outside this decision; queuing does not replace the per-seat exclusivity check. This record decides temporary seat ownership, not payment pricing or refund rules. Operators distinguish creation latency, assignment correctness, and catalog availability rather than treating any one as proof of the others. These facts and rationales are the complete authoritative basis for the synthetic record.
draft:
# ADR: Server-authoritative holds for Seatforge

**Status:** Accepted for the five-venue pilot.

## Context

Seatforge needs a precise boundary between seeing a seat in the catalog and temporarily owning the right to check out that seat. Several buyers can inspect the same performance, and a readable catalog does not establish which buyer has an active hold. This decision concerns temporary seat ownership. Payment pricing and refund rules are outside its scope.

The invariant is one active hold per seat within a particular performance. The performance qualification matters: the same physical seat can belong to separate performances without creating a double assignment. Review assignment correctness against the seat-and-performance pair rather than against a seat label alone.

## Decision

Use a server-authoritative hold with a standard duration of 120 seconds. The server clock determines when the hold expires. A browser countdown is a display of that deadline, not an independent authority that can lengthen the buyer's ownership. Different client clocks must not create different answers about whether the same hold is still active.

A retry with the same hold token returns the original result. It does not extend the original deadline. Replaying an expired hold therefore cannot revive ownership of the seat.

Creating a new hold requires a write quorum. If that quorum is lost, refuse new hold creation while keeping the seat catalog readable. The catalog remains useful for browsing, but its availability must not be represented as evidence that a purchase can acquire a hold.

## Checkout boundary

A checkout succeeds against the hold only if payment authorization was recorded before expiration. The relevant event is the recorded authorization, not the arrival time of the completion message. A completion message may arrive after the deadline and still succeed when its authorization was already recorded in time. Conversely, a browser that still displays time remaining cannot make a late authorization valid.

This distinction gives support staff a specific question to investigate: was the authorization recorded before the server's expiry boundary? It avoids turning a delayed message into proof that the buyer lost a valid authorization. The rule also keeps message delivery timing separate from the duration granted by the hold itself.

## Alternatives considered

We rejected browser-owned deadlines. A client display is useful feedback, but it cannot provide a shared clock for competing buyers. Letting each client determine expiration would make the exclusivity boundary depend on which device reported its time. The adopted server deadline gives the hold one authority that every request must respect.

We also rejected renewable standard holds. Repeated extension could keep a seat unavailable indefinitely, even though each individual extension looked bounded. A fixed hold makes the temporary allocation genuinely temporary. Buyers may need another opportunity after expiration, but replaying their original request is not that new opportunity.

Selling from cached catalog availability during a quorum outage was rejected as well. A catalog read is an observation; it cannot enforce that no competing hold exists. Maintaining browsing during an outage is valuable, but converting that observation into ownership would abandon the invariant the design is meant to preserve.

A global queue is outside this decision. Queuing buyers could influence who reaches the hold service first, but it would not replace the check on the particular seat and performance. The pilot should evaluate the chosen ownership rule without treating an unspecified queue as an additional correctness mechanism.

## Accessibility and scope

Only venue coordinators may create accessibility holds. Those holds last 240 seconds and cannot be renewed. The longer initial duration is a distinct policy, not a way to append time to an ordinary hold. Accessibility holds otherwise use the same exclusivity, server-clock, and token-replay rules as standard holds.

Bulk seat blocks are excluded from the pilot. Coordinators should not interpret the accessibility provision as approval for a group-allocation workflow. The pilot decision covers the stated hold types; evaluating a separate block-allocation policy would require its own scope and reasoning.

## Integration consequences

A retry with the same hold token returns the original result. It does not extend the original deadline. Replaying an expired hold therefore cannot revive ownership of the seat.

The token-to-hold mapping remains available for 24 hours after creation. That retention period is for recognizing the original request, not for keeping the seat held for a day. Reusing the token for a different seat produces `HOLD_KEY_CONFLICT`. Integrators must distinguish repeating an uncertain request from asking to acquire a different seat.

Hold tokens exclude buyer email. Use the token when tracing a request instead of turning an email address into the request's identity. The tracing convention should remain compatible with investigating a replay or a conflicting seat request without changing the ownership rule.

## Pilot evidence and expansion

The pilot includes five venues. Measure hold-creation latency at a sustained load of 600 requests per second; the acceptance gate is p95 no greater than 180 ms. This measures the creation path, so a responsive catalog cannot substitute for the required hold-creation result.

Expansion also requires seven consecutive days with zero double assignments. For this gate, a double assignment means overlapping active holds for the same seat and performance. A fast response is not evidence that this correctness condition held, and a clean assignment record is not evidence that the latency target was met. Both observations have their own role in the rollout decision.

## Operator review

Expiry is decided by the service's time source, even when the buyer's device shows a different countdown. Client-side time is advisory because devices cannot collectively establish one expiration instant. Use the server deadline when interpreting whether the hold was active.

During the pilot, distinguish creation latency, assignment correctness, and catalog availability in incident notes. A browsing success during a quorum outage is compatible with refused hold creation. Likewise, token recognition after the hold expired says that the original request can be identified; it does not say that the buyer still owns the seat.
